name: Rotating the List Values to the Left by One Position
description: Construct a program that has a function that receives a list of values and returns the list rotated to the left by 1 position so that the value at the front of the list goes to the back and the order of the other values stays the same. For example, if the list is [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], the program will change it to [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1].
code:
#Step 1: Define the function
def rotate_left(lst):
    #Step 1.1: Store the value at the front in a local variable
    first = lst[0] 
    #Step 1.2: Rotate the remaining values of the list to the left 
    for i in range(len(lst)-1):
        lst[i] = lst[i + 1]
    #Step 1.3: Move the value at the front to the back of the list
    lst[len(lst)-1] = first    
    return lst
#Step 2: Call the function
values =  [3, 8, 9, 8, 7, 5]
print("Original list:", values)
print("Rotated list: ", rotate_left(values))

How it affects data: the name lst becomes a local reference to the same list object you pass in — you do not get an automatic copy. That means the code inside can change the original list unless you explicitly copy it.

Alternatives worth knowing: you can implement the same behavior without mutating using slicing (lst[1:] + lst[:1]) or use collections.deque.rotate for efficiency on large lists — choose based on whether you want to modify the original list or create a new one.

commentList: Purpose: this line starts a loop that walks through each index from the front of the list up to the second-to-last item so you can copy the next item into the current position and thereby shift values left.
Syntax breakdown: 'for i in range(len(lst)-1):' makes i take the values 0, 1, ..., len(lst)-2. range(n) yields 0..n-1, and len(lst)-1 ensures the loop stops before the last index.
How it works with the code: you use i as the current index so the body can do lst[i] = lst[i+1]. Stopping at len(lst)-2 guarantees lst[i+1] is always a valid index (you won't read past the end).

Common errors and misconceptions: if you used range(len(lst)) instead, when i equals len(lst)-1 the expression lst[i+1] would try to access lst[len(lst)] and raise an IndexError. Also remember that if lst is empty, line 4 (first = lst[0]) already raises an error, so this loop won't protect you from that.

Edge cases to note: when len(lst) is 1, range(len(lst)-1) becomes range(0) and the loop body never runs — that's correct because there is nothing to shift. When len(lst) is 0, range(-1) is empty, but you must still handle the earlier access to lst[0].

Best practices: before this loop you should check for an empty list (for example: if not lst: return lst) to avoid IndexError. Consider using a clearer variable name (like index) or a slice-based alternative (lst[1:]+lst[:1]) if you prefer more readable code. Also decide whether you want to modify the original list in place (this code does) or return a new rotated list.

distractors.description: You might pick this because it feels natural to iterate over every index of the list. If you think every slot needs to be updated once, using range(len(lst)) seems right. However, with the rest of the code unchanged (which uses lst[i + 1] inside the loop), this causes the loop to try to read lst[len(lst)] on the final iteration. That index does not exist and Python raises an IndexError at runtime. In other words, you run one iteration too many. The mistake is an off-by-one error: the loop runs for the last index when it should stop before trying to access i+1. Replacing the correct loop with this line therefore makes the program crash instead of producing a rotated list.

You might pick this because it looks like you're moving the value at the current position forward into the next position. Step-by-step, what happens if you use this: on the first loop pass you copy the first element into the second slot, then on the next pass you copy that same value into the third slot, and so on. As the loop continues you overwrite later elements with earlier ones. After the loop finishes, the final step (which moves the saved front value to the back) will make many entries identical, so the list ends up filled with the same value instead of being rotated. This line is invalid for the intended left-rotation because it propagates values in the wrong direction — you are copying each element into the following slot rather than bringing the next element into the current slot — so the relative order is destroyed instead of shifted left.

You might choose this because it seems intuitive to fill the current position from the previous one. However, on the first iteration i is 0, so this accesses lst[-1] (the last element) and assigns it to the first slot. Then that value gets copied to subsequent positions, so you quickly get many copies of the last element. After the loop finishes and the saved first element is placed at the end, the list's order is wrong (for example, many positions will contain the old last value). This is incorrect for left-rotation because it uses the element behind the current index (and unintentionally uses Python's wrap-around negative index) instead of moving the next-in-line value into the current position.
